subject: Hierarchies in a seemingly unrelated regression?

messages.author: 45012a2c12a7d946
messages.subject: Hierarchies in a seemingly unrelated regression?
parts:
Dear Stan users,

I am trying to model some administrative agency data; I have a vector of three budgetary measures, so I want to fit a seemingly unrelated regression, but with levels to denote the agency the budget belongs to, with (ultimately) group level predictors based on the agency type. Ultimately I am aiming for something like the varying interval, varying slope with correlated group level predictors in Gelman and Hill S. 17.2, but I am trying to start of slowly and build myself up to there.

When I fit a simple SUR model with no agency-level variation, it works fine. So I tried to add a varying intercept, as a first stage. As far as I could work out, this involved the following changes, from a simple SUR:

In the data block,  I add int <lower=1> agency [N_obs]; and int<lower=1> J_agencies
In the parameters block, vector [3] a; becomes vector [3] a [J_agencies];
In the model block, y_hat[i] <- a + b * year[i]; becomes y_hat[i] <- a[agency[i]] + b * year[i];

This gives the following:

data {
                int<lower=0> N_obs;
                vector[3] y[N_obs];
                int<lower=2006,upper=2010> year [N_obs];
                int <lower=1> agency [N_obs];
                int<lower=1> J_agencies;
                }
       
        parameters {             
                vector <lower=-1, upper=1> [3] rho_sur;
                vector <lower=0> [3] sigma_sur;
                vector [3] a [J_agencies];
                vector [3] b;
                }
        transformed parameters{
                cov_matrix[3] Sigma_sur;
                Sigma_sur[1,1] <- square(sigma_sur[1]);
                Sigma_sur[2,2] <- square(sigma_sur[2]);
                Sigma_sur[3,3] <- square(sigma_sur[3]);
                Sigma_sur[1,2] <- rho_sur[1]*sigma_sur[1]*sigma_sur[2];
                Sigma_sur[1,3] <- rho_sur[2]*sigma_sur[1]*sigma_sur[3];
                Sigma_sur[2,3] <- rho_sur[3]*sigma_sur[2]*sigma_sur[3];
                Sigma_sur[2,1] <- Sigma_sur[1,2];
                Sigma_sur[3,1] <- Sigma_sur[1,3];
                Sigma_sur[3,2] <- Sigma_sur[2,3];
                }
        model {
                vector [3] y_hat [N_obs];
                a ~ normal (0, 10);
                b ~ normal (0, 10);
               for (i in 1:N_obs){
                y_hat[i] <- a[agency[i]] + b * year[i];
                    }
                y ~ multi_normal(y_hat, Sigma_sur);
                }

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchies in a seemingly unrelated regression?
parts:
Vectorization doesn’t work on an array of vectors — you need
to address each component of a independently by changing
a ~ normal (mu_a, sigma_a);

to

for (j in 1:J_agencies)
  a[j] ~ normal (mu_a, sigma_a);

Those normal(0, 100) priors aren’t helping anything (figure out
a reasonable scale for the standard deviation, not just a big one)
and if the covariance matrix gets any bigger you’ll probably want
to look into parameterizing the Cholesky factor directly (see
recent email threads).

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchies in a seemingly unrelated regression?
parts: Finally figured it out, after studying further the ARM example models, and after some advice from a friend about the way arrays and vectors work in Stan. For posterity, the code below works, I think. It could be faster if I made better use of matrices and vectors, but I was aiming for clear (to me) code above all.

data {
          int<lower=1> N_obs;
          int<lower=1> J_agencies;

vector[3] y [N_obs];
          int <lower=2006,upper=2010> year [N_obs];
int <lower=0> agency [N_obs];

}
     
    parameters {           
           vector <lower=-1, upper=1> [3] rho_sur;

vector <lower=0, upper=10> [3] sigma_sur;
           vector <lower=0, upper=10> [3] sigma_a;
           vector <lower=0, upper=10> [3] sigma_b;

vector <lower=-1, upper=1> [3] rho;
           vector [3] mu_a;
           vector [3] mu_b;
vector [2] B_temp [3];

}
                                                              
     transformed parameters{
             cov_matrix[3] Sigma_sur;
             Sigma_sur[1,1] <- square(sigma_sur[1]);
             Sigma_sur[2,2] <- square(sigma_sur[2]);
             Sigma_sur[3,3] <- square(sigma_sur[3]);
             Sigma_sur[1,2] <- rho_sur[1]*sigma_sur[1]*sigma_sur[2];
             Sigma_sur[1,3] <- rho_sur[2]*sigma_sur[1]*sigma_sur[3];
             Sigma_sur[2,3] <- rho_sur[3]*sigma_sur[2]*sigma_sur[3];
             Sigma_sur[2,1] <- Sigma_sur[1,2];
             Sigma_sur[3,1] <- Sigma_sur[1,3];
             Sigma_sur[3,2] <- Sigma_sur[2,3];
                                }
                                                              
       model {
            vector [3] y_hat [N_obs];
            vector [3] a [J_agencies];

vector [3] b [J_agencies];
            matrix [J_agencies, 2] B_hat [3];
            matrix [2,2] Sigma_b [3];
            matrix [J_agencies, 2] B [3];
           
            mu_a ~ normal(0, 100);
            mu_b ~ normal(0, 100);
                           
                     
              for(n in 1:3){
                      Sigma_b[n][1,1] <- pow(sigma_a[n], 2);
                      Sigma_b[n][2,2] <- pow(sigma_b[n], 2);
                      Sigma_b[n][1,2] <- rho[n] * sigma_a[n] * sigma_b[n];
                      Sigma_b[n][2,1] <- Sigma_b[n][1,2];
                        for(j in 1:J_agencies){
                               B_hat[n][j, 1] <- mu_a[n];
                            B_hat[n][j, 2] <- mu_b[n];
                            B_temp[n] ~ multi_normal(transpose(row(B_hat[n],j)), Sigma_b[n]);
                            B[n][j,1] <- B_temp[n][1];
                            B[n][j,2] <- B_temp[n][2]; 
                            a[j][n] <- B[n][j,1];
                            b[j][n] <- B[n][j,2];

}
                                            }

                                                                
            for (i in 1:N_obs){

y_hat[i] <- a[agency[i]] + b[agency[i]] * year[i];
                                  }     
                 y ~ multi_normal(y_hat, Sigma_sur);
     }

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Hierarchies in a seemingly unrelated regression?
parts:
Thanks for sharing.

The biggest problem I see in this code is that
there's no guarantee that Sigma_sur will be positive
definite as constructed. When it's not, you just get
rejections and the sampler can devolve to a random walk.

The best thing to do for efficiency is to use a cholesky
factor basis for covariance matrix parameters like Sigma_sur
and then scale it. There's a discussion in the 2.5.0 manual.
And also more advice on priors for scales --- we no longer recommend
uniform(0,10) or similar priors for techically unconstrained variables
(by which I mean variables for which there would be support outside of
their constrained values). Those normal(0,100) priors probably
aren't doing much either --- we also discuss those in the
new manual and recommend either just going all the way to
an improper uniform prior or adding some information.

You could do the same thing for the temp covariance matrix
Sigma_b, though there would be a speedup from just Cholesky
factoring what you have before the loop. You could even
do that analytically since you know the matrix is 2 x 2 and
positive definite.

You can write B[n][j,1] as B[n,j,1], and the latter may be
a bit more efficient, but I can see why someone might prefer
the former for clarity.

- Bob

On Oct 23, 2014, at 10:30 AM, Lindsay <lindsay...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Finally figured it out, after studying further the ARM example models, and after some advice from a friend about the way arrays and vectors work in Stan. For posterity, the code below works, I think. It could be faster if I made better use of matrices and vectors, but I was aiming for clear (to me) code above all.
>
> data {
> int<lower=1> N_obs;
> int<lower=1> J_agencies;
> vector[3] y [N_obs];
> int <lower=2006,upper=2010> year [N_obs];
> int <lower=0> agency [N_obs];
> }
>
> parameters {
> vector <lower=-1, upper=1> [3] rho_sur;
> vector <lower=0, upper=10> [3] sigma_sur;
> vector <lower=0, upper=10> [3] sigma_a;
> vector <lower=0, upper=10> [3] sigma_b;
> vector <lower=-1, upper=1> [3] rho;
> vector [3] mu_a;
> vector [3] mu_b;
> vector [2] B_temp [3];
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
> cov_matrix[3] Sigma_sur;
> Sigma_sur[1,1] <- square(sigma_sur[1]);
> Sigma_sur[2,2] <- square(sigma_sur[2]);
> Sigma_sur[3,3] <- square(sigma_sur[3]);
> Sigma_sur[1,2] <- rho_sur[1]*sigma_sur[1]*sigma_sur[2];
> Sigma_sur[1,3] <- rho_sur[2]*sigma_sur[1]*sigma_sur[3];
> Sigma_sur[2,3] <- rho_sur[3]*sigma_sur[2]*sigma_sur[3];
> Sigma_sur[2,1] <- Sigma_sur[1,2];
> Sigma_sur[3,1] <- Sigma_sur[1,3];
> Sigma_sur[3,2] <- Sigma_sur[2,3];
> }
>
> model {
> vector [3] y_hat [N_obs];
> vector [3] a [J_agencies];
> vector [3] b [J_agencies];
> matrix [J_agencies, 2] B_hat [3];
> matrix [2,2] Sigma_b [3];
> matrix [J_agencies, 2] B [3];
>
> mu_a ~ normal(0, 100);
> mu_b ~ normal(0, 100);
>
>
> for(n in 1:3){
> Sigma_b[n][1,1] <- pow(sigma_a[n], 2);
> Sigma_b[n][2,2] <- pow(sigma_b[n], 2);
> Sigma_b[n][1,2] <- rho[n] * sigma_a[n] * sigma_b[n];
> Sigma_b[n][2,1] <- Sigma_b[n][1,2];
> for(j in 1:J_agencies){
> B_hat[n][j, 1] <- mu_a[n];
> B_hat[n][j, 2] <- mu_b[n];
> B_temp[n] ~ multi_normal(transpose(row(B_hat[n],j)), Sigma_b[n]);
> B[n][j,1] <- B_temp[n][1];
> B[n][j,2] <- B_temp[n][2];
> a[j][n] <- B[n][j,1];
> b[j][n] <- B[n][j,2];
> }
> }
>
>
> for (i in 1:N_obs){
> y_hat[i] <- a[agency[i]] + b[agency[i]] * year[i];
> }
> y ~ multi_normal(y_hat, Sigma_sur);
> }
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Hierarchies in a seemingly unrelated regression?
parts:
Thanks, Bob,

I've read the Stan manual on Cholesky decomposition. Would I be right in thinking that in Stan this would be as simple as re-writing the transformed parameters block as:

 transformed parameters{
         cov_matrix[3] Sigma;
         matrix[3, 3] L;
         Sigma[1,1] <- square(sigma[1]);
         Sigma[2,2] <- square(sigma[2]);
         Sigma[3,3] <- square(sigma[3]);
         Sigma[1,2] <- rho[1]*sigma[1]*sigma[2];
         Sigma[1,3] <- rho[2]*sigma[1]*sigma[3];
         Sigma[2,3] <- rho[3]*sigma[2]*sigma[3];
         Sigma[2,1] <- Sigma[1,2];
         Sigma[3,1] <- Sigma[1,3];
         Sigma[3,2] <- Sigma[2,3];
         L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
                            }

...and rewriting the last line as:

y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(y_hat, L);

?

Thanks,

Lindsay

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Hierarchies in a seemingly unrelated regression?
parts:
Yes that will work as far as the Cholesky's concerned, but
it doesn't solve the major problem, which is that there's
no guarantee with this construction that Sigma is positive
definite. It also won't improve efficiency if there's only
a single sampling statement (rather than a loop of them).

So what I'm suggesting is use a cholesky_factor_corr as a parameter,
provide an lkj_corr prior on that, have the same sigma[] array
with whatever priors you want, then use the quad form to put
it all together. There's an example in the 2.5 manual in the
regression chapter in a section on multivariate priors.

- Bob
